lesson: Vomiting and deep breathing — a DKA reasoning case
voice_profile: Mature British male paediatric medical lecturer. Warm, calm, clear and conversational. Teach rather than read the screen. Pause after questions so the learner can think. Each narration belongs only to the current case step and should make sense independently.

stages.script: Here is the patient. A twelve-year-old with three days of increasing thirst and frequent urination. Since yesterday there has been vomiting, abdominal discomfort and lethargy, and today the breathing has become strikingly deep and rapid. The child is tachycardic and clinically dehydrated, but the oxygen saturation is ninety-nine percent. Before you think of a diagnosis, ask a more useful question: what needs explaining? In particular, which feature makes simple gastroenteritis an incomplete explanation? Look at the choices on screen and make your decision before continuing.

Now build the problem rather than naming the disease. We have thirst, polyuria and dehydration, followed by vomiting and deep breathing. The normal oxygen saturation is important. The lungs are moving a lot of air, but there is no obvious failure of oxygenation. So perhaps the breathing is a response to a problem elsewhere. Try to find one mechanism that can connect excessive urination, volume loss and this unusual respiratory pattern. Keep that hypothesis in mind, then continue to the investigations.

Now we test the mechanism. The glucose is twenty-eight millimoles per litre and blood ketones are five point six. The pH is seven point one two and bicarbonate is eight, so there is a substantial metabolic acidosis. Carbon dioxide is low because ventilation has increased to compensate. Notice that the potassium is four point eight. That serum value does not mean total body potassium is normal; osmotic diuresis causes potassium loss, while insulin deficiency and acidaemia can keep potassium in the extracellular space. Before revealing the diagnosis, identify the acid-base disturbance on screen. Once you have done that, reveal the diagnosis and continue.

We now know this is diabetic ketoacidosis. But recognising the name is not the same as understanding it. Start with the missing signal: insulin. Without enough insulin, glucose cannot be used normally by insulin-sensitive tissues, while hepatic glucose production continues. Blood glucose rises. Once the renal threshold is exceeded, glucose remains in the tubular fluid, water follows it, and osmotic diuresis develops. At the same time, the loss of insulin removes the brake on lipolysis. Free fatty acids reach the liver and are converted into ketone bodies. Those ketones are acids and bicarbonate is consumed buffering them. One missing hormone therefore creates two linked problems: hyperglycaemic volume loss and ketoacidosis.

Now make the clinical picture cohere. Polyuria comes from glycosuria and osmotic diuresis. Thirst is the physiological response to that water loss. Dehydration and falling effective circulating volume explain the tachycardia. Ketosis, acidaemia and dehydration contribute to the vomiting and abdominal pain. And the deep breathing is not primarily a lung problem. Falling pH stimulates ventilation, carbon dioxide is blown off, and the respiratory system partially compensates for the metabolic acidosis. That is why Kussmaul breathing belongs naturally in this case. Each finding can now be derived from the mechanism rather than memorised as part of a list.

Treatment now becomes physiology in reverse. Fluids restore effective circulation, renal perfusion and the water deficit. Insulin is essential not merely because it lowers glucose, but because it switches off lipolysis and ketone production. Potassium needs active attention because total body stores are depleted and insulin will drive potassium back into cells. Glucose may fall before the ketoacidosis has resolved. When that happens, dextrose can be added so insulin can continue safely until ketogenesis is suppressed. Neurological observations remain important because cerebral injury is a serious complication. Exact fluid, insulin, electrolyte and monitoring decisions should always follow the current paediatric DKA guideline.

Now reconstruct the whole patient from the beginning. Insulin deficiency produces hyperglycaemia and removes the restraint on lipolysis. Hyperglycaemia causes glycosuria, osmotic diuresis, dehydration, thirst and tachycardia. Lipolysis supplies fatty acids to the liver, ketone production rises, bicarbonate falls and metabolic acidosis develops. The lungs compensate by lowering carbon dioxide through deep rapid breathing. Investigations measure different parts of that causal chain, and treatment reverses it. If you can rebuild that story from insulin deficiency to the child's presentation, you understand the case rather than simply remembering DKA features. Continue once more for optional references and deeper learning.
